etymologies.etymologyHTML: Borrowed from Late Latin īrōnicus, from Ancient Greek εἰρωνικός (eirōnikós). Compare Middle French, ironique, equivalent to irony +‎ -ic.

definitions.definition: (Of a situation) Characterized by or constituting (any kind of) irony.

quote.citation: 2014, Steven Pinker, The Sense of Style: The Thinking Person's Guide to Writing in the 21st Century!, page 275:
quote.text: It was ironic I forgot my textbook on human memory.

quote.citation: 2009 October 29, David Walliams [pseudonym; David Edward Williams], Mr Stink, London: HarperCollins Children’s Books, →ISBN:
quote.text: Chloe had once seen a real-life goth hanging around by a garbage bin in the high street and become incredibly excited. She really wanted to go over and ask her how to get started in the goth world, but she was too shy. Which was ironic, since shyness is something you need if you want to be a successful goth.

definitions.definition: (preceded with "being") Acting in an unserious and teasing manner.
(Of a statement, action, etc.) Done in an insincere and mocking manner; satirical.
